input.command:
python3 << 'EOF'
from PIL import Image
import numpy as np

img = Image.open('barcode.png').convert('RGB')
a = np.asarray(img).astype(float)
col_avg = a.mean(axis=0)  # (1000,3)
lum = col_avg.mean(axis=1)

# Where are the brightest stripes?
order = np.argsort(lum)[::-1]
print("Top 30 brightest stripes (x, RGB, lum):")
seen = []
for i in order[:60]:
    x = int(i)
    if all(abs(x-s) > 8 for s in seen):
        seen.append(x)
        rgb = col_avg[x].round(0).astype(int)
        print(f"x={x:4d}  RGB={tuple(rgb)}  lum={lum[x]:.0f}  (t={x*0.1:.1f}% of runtime)")
    if len(seen) >= 15: break

# Tint analysis: which stripes are notably blue vs warm
r,g,b = col_avg[:,0], col_avg[:,1], col_avg[:,2]
blue_excess = b - (r+g)/2
warm_excess = r - (g+b)/2
print("\nMost blue-tinted stripes:")
for i in np.argsort(blue_excess)[::-1][:8]:
    print(f"  x={i:4d} RGB={col_avg[i].round(0).astype(int)} blue_excess={blue_excess[i]:.1f}")
print("Most warm/red-tinted stripes:")
for i in np.argsort(warm_excess)[::-1][:8]:
    print(f"  x={i:4d} RGB={col_avg[i].round(0).astype(int)} warm_excess={warm_excess[i]:.1f}")
print("Most green-tinted stripes:")
green_excess = g - (r+b)/2
for i in np.argsort(green_excess)[::-1][:8]:
    print(f"  x={i:4d} RGB={col_avg[i].round(0).astype(int)} green_excess={green_excess[i]:.1f}")

# Fraction of near-black stripes
print("\n% stripes with lum<5:", (lum<5).mean()*100)
print("% stripes with lum<10:", (lum<10).mean()*100)
print("% stripes with lum>60:", (lum>60).mean()*100)
print("% stripes with lum>100:", (lum>100).mean()*100)

# Saturation stats (max-min channel)
sat = col_avg.max(axis=1) - col_avg.min(axis=1)
print("mean channel spread (saturation proxy):", sat.mean().round(2))
EOF

***Night of the Living Dead*** is a 1968 American [zombie horror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zombie_horror "Zombie horror") film directed, photographed, and edited by [George A. Romero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_A._Romero "George A. Romero"), written by Romero and [John Russo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_A._Russo "John A. Russo"), and produced by [Russell W. Streiner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Streiner "Russell Streiner") and Karl Hardman. The [independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_film "Independent film") film's [ensemble cast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ensemble_cast "Ensemble cast")—which includes [Duane Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duane_Jones "Duane Jones"), [Judith O'Dea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_O'Dea "Judith O'Dea"), [Marilyn Eastman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marilyn_Eastman "Marilyn Eastman"), Karl Hardman, Judith Ridley, and Keith Wayne—star as a group of people trapped in a farmhouse in rural [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania"), under assault by flesh-eating [reanimated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undead "Undead") corpses. Although the monsters that appear in the film are referred to as "[ghouls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghoul "Ghoul")", they are credited with popularizing the modern portrayal of [zombies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zombie "Zombie") in popular culture.

Having gained experience creating television commercials, [industrial films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_film "Industrial film"), and *[Mister Rogers' Neighborhood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mister_Rogers'_Neighborhood "Mister Rogers' Neighborhood")* segments through their production company The Latent Image, Romero, Russo, and Streiner decided to make a horror film to capitalize on interest in the genre. Their script primarily drew inspiration from [Richard Matheson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Matheson "Richard Matheson")'s 1954 novel *[I Am Legend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Am_Legend_\(novel\) "I Am Legend (novel)")*. [Principal photography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_photography "Principal photography") took place between July 1967 and January 1968, mainly on location in [Evans City, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evans_City,_Pennsylvania "Evans City, Pennsylvania"), with Romero using [guerrilla filmmaking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guerrilla_filmmaking "Guerrilla filmmaking") techniques he had honed in his commercial and industrial work to complete the film on a [budget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_budgeting "Film budgeting") of approximately US$100,000. Unable to procure a proper set, the crew rented a condemned farmhouse to destroy during the course of filming.

*Night of the Living Dead* premiered in Pittsburgh on October 1, 1968\. It grossed US$12 million [domestically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_of_the_United_States "Cinema of the United States") and US$18 million internationally, earning more than 250 times its budget and making it one of the most profitable film productions of all time. Released shortly before the adoption of the [Motion Picture Association of America rating system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_Picture_Association_film_rating_system "Motion Picture Association film rating system"), the film's explicit violence and gore were considered groundbreaking, leading to controversy and negative reviews. It eventually garnered a [cult following](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult_film "Cult film") and critical acclaim, and has appeared on lists of [the greatest and most influential films ever made](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_films_considered_the_best "List of films considered the best") by such outlets as *[Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_\(magazine\) "Empire (magazine)")*, *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")* and *[Total Film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_Film "Total Film")*. Frequently identified as a touchstone in the development of the horror genre, retrospective scholarly analysis has focused on its reflection of the social and cultural changes in the United States during the 1960s, with particular attention towards the casting of Jones, an African-American, in the leading role.[\[6\]](#cite_note-Anarchy-8) In 1999, the film was deemed "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant" by the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") and selected for preservation in the [National Film Registry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Film_Registry "National Film Registry").[\[7\]](#cite_note-CNN-9)[\[8\]](#cite_note-PM-10)[\[9\]](#cite_note-11)

*Night of the Living Dead* created a successful [franchise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night_of_the_Living_Dead_\(film_series\) "Night of the Living Dead (film series)") that includes five following films released between 1978 and 2009, all directed by Romero. Since the film was mistakenly created without a [copyright notice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright_notice "Copyright notice"), it entered the [public domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_domain "Public domain") upon release,[\[10\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBolukLenz20115-12) resulting in numerous adaptations, [remakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remake "Remake"), and a lasting legacy in the horror genre. An [official remake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night_of_the_Living_Dead_\(1990_film\) "Night of the Living Dead (1990 film)"), written by Romero and directed by [Tom Savini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Savini "Tom Savini"), was released in 1990\.

## Plot

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Night_of_the_Living_Dead&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")\]

*Night of the Living Dead* (1968)

Siblings Barbra and Johnny Blair drive to a cemetery in rural [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania") to visit their father's grave, where a pale man in a tattered suit kills Johnny and attacks Barbra. Fleeing to a nearby farmhouse, she finds the resident's corpse lying half-eaten on the stairs. A growing horde of ghouls surrounds the house as a stranger, Ben, arrives and initially mistakes Barbra for the homeowner. After driving back several ghouls, he boards the windows and doors. A traumatized Barbra falls into a near catatonic state, forcing Ben to look after her. While searching the home for supplies, he locates a [lever-action rifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winchester_Model_1894 "Winchester Model 1894") upstairs.

Barbra is surprised to find people already taking shelter in the home's cellar. Harry Cooper, his wife Helen, and their young daughter Karen fled there after ghouls overturned their car and bit Karen on the arm, leaving her seriously ill. A teenage couple, Tom and Judy, took shelter after hearing an emergency broadcast while they were at a nearby lake. Tom and Ben secure the farmhouse while Harry protests that it is unsafe aboveground, before returning to the cellar. Tension rises in the group as more of the ghouls arrive to besiege the farmhouse.

Through radio and TV reports, the survivors learn that cannibalistic corpses, referred to as "ghouls", are reanimating and committing [mass murder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_murder "Mass murder") across the [East Coast of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Coast_of_the_United_States "East Coast of the United States") and that [posses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Posse_comitatus "Posse comitatus") of armed men are patrolling the countryside to exterminate the living dead. Reports confirm that the ghouls can die again from heavy blows to the head, bullets to the brain, or being burned. Various rescue centers offer refuge and safety, and scientists theorize that [radiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiation "Radiation") from an exploding [space probe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_probe "Space probe") returning from [Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus "Venus") caused the reanimations.

Ben devises a plan to obtain medical supplies for Karen and transport the group to a rescue center by refueling his truck at a pump on the farm. Ben, Tom, and Judy drive there together, holding the ghouls off with torches and [Molotov cocktails](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molotov_cocktail "Molotov cocktail"). However, spilled gasoline catches fire and causes the truck to explode, killing Tom and Judy. Ben makes it back, but when Harry refuses to unlock the door, Ben breaks it down.

The remaining survivors debate possible options, pausing when the 3 a.m. news broadcast airs. As they watch the update, the power fails, and the ghouls break through the doors and windows of the unlit home. In the chaos, Harry grabs Ben's gun to threaten him, but is disarmed and shot by Ben. Harry staggers down to the cellar and dies beside his daughter. Barbra awakens from her delirium and saves Helen from the ghouls, who then flees to the cellar.

Karen dies from her injuries, becomes a ghoul, feeds on her father's remains, and stabs her mother to death with a masonry [trowel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trowel "Trowel"). Barbra tries to help Ben keep the ghouls out, but freezes upon seeing the reanimated Johnny, who drags her into the horde. As the horde pours into the farmhouse, Ben retreats to the cellar, where he shoots the reanimated Harry and Helen.

In the morning, an armed posse arrives to dispatch the remaining ghouls. Awakened by their gunfire, Ben emerges from the cellar, but, mistaking him for a ghoul, the posse shoots him. His body is thrown onto a bonfire and burned with the other corpses.

[![Ben holds a rifle in the farmhouse living room.](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/31/Duane_Jones_NLD.jpg/250px-Duane_Jones_NLD.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Duane_Jones_NLD.jpg)

Ben, played by [Duane Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duane_Jones "Duane Jones")

[![Judy peers from an open truck window.](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/JudithRidley.jpg/250px-JudithRidley.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:JudithRidley.jpg)

Judith Ridley as Judy, near the gas pump

The low-budget film featured no well-known actors,[\[11\]](#cite_note-Sandell2017-13) but it propelled several cast members' careers.[\[12\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane2010ch. 4-14) Two independent film companies from [Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh "Pittsburgh")—Hardman Associates and director [George A. Romero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_A._Romero "George A. Romero")'s The Latent Image—combined to form Image Ten, a production company chartered only to create *Night of the Living Dead*.[\[13\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201020–23-15) The cast consisted of members of Image Ten; actors previously cast in their commercials; clients who commissioned commercials; local TV, radio, and law enforcement; acquaintances of Romero, production crew and their relatives; and Pittsburgh stage actors.[\[14\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane2010ch. 4,_pp. 42–48-16)

- [Duane Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duane_Jones "Duane Jones") as Ben. The casting was potentially controversial in 1968 when it was rare for a black actor to be cast as the hero of an American film with a predominantly white cast, but Romero said Jones gave the best audition.[\[15\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones2005118-17) Jones later appeared in other films, including *[Ganja & Hess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganja_&_Hess "Ganja & Hess")* (1973) and *[Beat Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_Street "Beat Street")* (1984).[\[16\]](#cite_note-18)

- [Judith O'Dea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_O'Dea "Judith O'Dea") as Barbra Blair. A 23-year-old commercial and stage actress, O'Dea had previously worked for Hardman and Eastman in Pittsburgh. She was in Hollywood pursuing a film career when contacted about the role.[\[17\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECollum20043–9-19) O'Dea expressed surprise at the film's cultural impact and the recognition it brought her.[\[18\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECollum20044-20)

- [Russell Streiner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Streiner "Russell Streiner") as Johnny Blair, Barbra's brother. Streiner, Romero's business partner at The Latent Image, was one of the film's producers.[\[19\]](#cite_note-image-ten-streiner-21) In the film's credits, he is listed solely as a producer. Despite having no prior film acting experience,[\[20\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERusso198542-22) Streiner went on to act in and produce other films, notably the [1990 remake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night_of_the_Living_Dead_\(1990_film\) "Night of the Living Dead (1990 film)"), where he also had a cameo appearance as Sheriff McClelland.[\[19\]](#cite_note-image-ten-streiner-21)[\[21\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane2010-23)

- Karl Hardman as Harry Cooper. Hardman was president of Hardman Associates and one of the film's producers. Cooper's wife was played by Hardman's real-life business and romantic partner, Marilyn Eastman.[\[22\]](#cite_note-24)[\[23\]](#cite_note-Barnes2021-25) Hardman also remixed the film's sound track and created sound effects.[\[24\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201071–72-26)

- [Marilyn Eastman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marilyn_Eastman "Marilyn Eastman") as Helen Cooper.[\[25\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECollum20043-27) Vice president of Hardman Associates, Marilyn Eastman played Helen Cooper and the unnamed, bug-eating zombie. She later appeared in *[Santa Claws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Claws_\(1996_film\) "Santa Claws (1996 film)")* (1996), directed by [John Russo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_A._Russo "John A. Russo").[\[23\]](#cite_note-Barnes2021-25)[\[26\]](#cite_note-28)

- Kyra Schon as Karen Cooper. Hardman's daughter in real life,[\[27\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201042-29) nine-year-old Schon also portrayed the mangled corpse on the house's upper floor that Ben drags away.[\[28\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201043-30)

- Keith Wayne as Tom. "Keith Wayne" was Ronald Keith Hartman's stage name.[\[28\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201043-30) After this lone acting role, Wayne went on to work as a singer, dancer, musician, and night-club owner,[\[29\]](#cite_note-news.google.com-31)[\[28\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201043-30) before becoming a [chiropractor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiropractor "Chiropractor") in North Carolina.[\[29\]](#cite_note-news.google.com-31) Wayne explained the change in careers during a 1992 interview, "I am not that person anymore. \[...\] I got to a point in my life where I wanted to have some control. I didn't want to wake up at 40 or 50 and not be in control."[\[30\]](#cite_note-32) In 1995, he took his own life at age 50\.[\[31\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane2010204-33)[\[32\]](#cite_note-34)

- Judith Ridley as Judy. A 19-year-old receptionist from Hardman Associates, Ridley auditioned for Barbra without any acting experience and was given the less-demanding role of Judy.[\[33\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201042–43-35) Ridley starred in Romero's second feature *[There's Always Vanilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/There's_Always_Vanilla "There's Always Vanilla")* (1971).[\[34\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201090–92-36)

- [Bill Hinzman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Hinzman "Bill Hinzman") as the cemetery ghoul. Hinzman played the first ghoul encountered by Barbra and Johnny in the cemetery and later worked on several horror films including *[The Majorettes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Majorettes "The Majorettes")* (1986) and *[Flesheater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flesheater "Flesheater")* (1988).[\[35\]](#cite_note-37)[\[36\]](#cite_note-38)

- [George Kosana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Kosana "George Kosana") as Sheriff McClelland. Kosana also served as the film's [production manager](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_production_manager "Unit production manager").[\[37\]](#cite_note-:0-39)

- [Bill "Chilly Billy" Cardille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Cardille "Bill Cardille") as himself.[\[38\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201045-40) Cardille was well known in Pittsburgh as the [horror host](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horror_host "Horror host") of the anthology series *[Chiller Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiller_Theatre_\(Pittsburgh\) "Chiller Theatre (Pittsburgh)")*.[\[39\]](#cite_note-41) His daughter [Lori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lori_Cardille "Lori Cardille") later starred in Romero's *[Day of the Dead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day_of_the_Dead_\(1985_film\) "Day of the Dead (1985 film)")* (1985).[\[40\]](#cite_note-42)[\[41\]](#cite_note-43)

## Production

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Night_of_the_Living_Dead&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Production")\]

### Development and pre-production

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Night_of_the_Living_Dead&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Development and pre-production")\]

External videos

[![video icon](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/Nuvola_apps_kaboodle.svg/20px-Nuvola_apps_kaboodle.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nuvola_apps_kaboodle.svg) [The Calgon Story](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1oMQRrcLIaI) The creation of this high-budget [television commercial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_commercial "Television commercial") for [Calgon water softener](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calgon "Calgon") spurred the film's producers to create *Night of the Living Dead*.[\[42\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201028-44)

George Romero embarked upon his career in the [film industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_industry "Film industry") while attending [Carnegie Mellon University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Mellon_University "Carnegie Mellon University") in [Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh "Pittsburgh").[\[43\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201025-45) He directed and produced television commercials and [industrial films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sponsored_film "Sponsored film") for The Latent Image, a company he co-founded with his friend [Russell Streiner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Streiner "Russell Streiner").[\[44\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201026–27-46) The Latent Image started small, but after producing a high-budget [Calgon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calgon "Calgon") commercial spoofing *[Fantastic Voyage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fantastic_Voyage "Fantastic Voyage")* (1966), Romero felt that the company had the experience and equipment to produce a feature film.[\[42\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201028-44) They wanted to capitalize on the film industry's "thirst for the bizarre", according to Romero.[\[45\]](#cite_note-47) He, Streiner, and [John A. Russo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_A._Russo "John A. Russo") contacted Karl Hardman and Marilyn Eastman, president, and vice president respectively, of a Pittsburgh-based industrial film firm called Hardman Associates, Inc. The Latent Image pitched their idea for a then-untitled horror film.[\[46\]](#cite_note-Hardman/Eastmaninterview-48)

These discussions led to the creation of Image Ten, a production company chartered to produce a single feature film. The initial budget was $6,000;[\[13\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201020–23-15) each member of the production company invested $600 for a share of the profits.[\[47\]](#cite_note-49)[\[c\]](#cite_note-50) Ten more investors contributed another $6,000, but this was still insufficient.[\[48\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERusso19856–7-51) Production stopped multiple times during filming while Romero used early footage to persuade additional investors.[\[49\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPeary1981227-52) Image Ten eventually raised approximately $114,000 for the budget ($1,055,000 today).[\[50\]](#cite_note-inflation-US-53)[\[48\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERusso19856–7-51)

### Writing

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Night_of_the_Living_Dead&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Writing")\]

[![A group of actors in zombie makeup shamble across the unlit lawn of the farmhouse.](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/Zombies_NightoftheLivingDead.jpg/250px-Zombies_NightoftheLivingDead.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Zombies_NightoftheLivingDead.jpg)

Ghouls swarm around the house, searching for living [human flesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_cannibalism "Human cannibalism").

The script was co-written by Russo and Romero. They abandoned an early [horror comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horror_comedy_\(genre\) "Horror comedy (genre)") concept about adolescent aliens,[\[51\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201023-54) after realizing they would not have the budget to create a convincing spaceship.[\[52\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201021-55) Russo proposed a more constrained narrative where a young man runs away from home and discovers aliens harvesting human corpses for food in a cemetery.[\[53\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERusso198531,_61-56)[\[54\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201020–24-57) Romero combined this idea with an unpublished short story about flesh-eating ghouls,[\[55\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBishop2006199-58) and they began filming with an incomplete script.[\[49\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPeary1981227-52)[\[51\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201023-54) According to Russo, the screenplay written prior to filming only covered events up to the emergence of the Cooper family.[\[56\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESurmacz197516-59) Russo completed the script while filming and Romero later expanded the final pages of his short story into the sequels *[Dawn of the Dead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawn_of_the_Dead_\(1978_film\) "Dawn of the Dead (1978 film)")* (1978) and *[Day of the Dead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day_of_the_Dead_\(1985_film\) "Day of the Dead (1985 film)")* (1985).[\[57\]](#cite_note-60)

Romero drew inspiration from [Richard Matheson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Matheson "Richard Matheson")'s *[I Am Legend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Am_Legend_\(novel\) "I Am Legend (novel)")* (1954),[\[58\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDinello2006257-61)[\[d\]](#cite_note-62) a [horror novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horror_fiction "Horror fiction") about a [plague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epidemic "Epidemic") that ravages a futuristic Los Angeles. The infected in *I Am Legend* become [vampire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vampire "Vampire")\-like creatures and prey on the uninfected.[\[59\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPaffenroth2006138–143-63)[\[48\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERusso19856–7-51)[\[60\]](#cite_note-64) Matheson described Romero's interpretation as "kind of cornball",[\[61\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeaver1999307-65) and more theft than homage.[\[62\]](#cite_note-66) In an interview, Romero contrasted *Night of the Living Dead* with *I Am Legend*. He explained that Matheson wrote about the aftermath of a complete global upheaval; Romero wanted to explore how people would respond to that kind of disaster as it developed.[\[63\]](#cite_note-67)

Much of the dialogue was altered, rewritten, or improvised by the cast.[\[64\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201033–34,_40,_45-68) Lead actress Judith O'Dea told an interviewer, "I don't know if there was an actual working script! We would go over what basically had to be done, then just did it the way we each felt it *should* be done".[\[18\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECollum20044-20) One example offered by O'Dea concerns a scene where Barbra tells Ben about Johnny's death. O'Dea said that the script vaguely had Barbra talk about riding in the car with Johnny before they were attacked. She described Barbra's dialogue for the scene as entirely [improv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Improv_theater "Improv theater").[\[65\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECollum20043–4-69) Eastman modified the scenes written for Helen and Harry Cooper in the cellar.[\[46\]](#cite_note-Hardman/Eastmaninterview-48) Karl Hardman attributed Ben's lines to lead actor Duane Jones. Ben was an uneducated truck driver in the script until Jones began to rewrite his character.[\[66\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201032–35-70)[\[46\]](#cite_note-Hardman/Eastmaninterview-48)

The lead role was initially written for a [white](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_American "White American") actor, but upon casting black actor Duane Jones, Romero intentionally did not alter the script to reflect this.[\[67\]](#cite_note-Walkdead-71) The film appeared in theaters at a time when very few black actors played leading roles. The rare exceptions, like the consciously black heroes played by [Sidney Poitier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidney_Poitier "Sidney Poitier"), were written as subservient to make those characters palatable to white audiences.[\[68\]](#cite_note-72)[\[69\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarper2005-73) Asked in 2013 if he took inspiration from the [assassination of Martin Luther King Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Martin_Luther_King_Jr. "Assassination of Martin Luther King Jr.") in the same year that the movie was made, Romero responded in the negative, noting that he only heard about the shooting when he was on his way to find distribution for the finished film.[\[67\]](#cite_note-Walkdead-71)

### Filming

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Night_of_the_Living_Dead&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Filming")\]

#### Principal photography

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Night_of_the_Living_Dead&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Principal photography")\]

[![Color photograph of tombstones from the film.](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/EvansCityCemetery_PA.jpg/250px-EvansCityCemetery_PA.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:EvansCityCemetery_PA.jpg)

[Evans City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evans_City,_Pennsylvania "Evans City, Pennsylvania") Cemetery in 2007

[![Color photograph of the cemetery chapel seen in the film, now with all windows boarded over.](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f6/Evans_City_Cemetery_Chapel%2C_Evans_City%2C_PA_-_February_2009.jpg/250px-Evans_City_Cemetery_Chapel%2C_Evans_City%2C_PA_-_February_2009.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Evans_City_Cemetery_Chapel,_Evans_City,_PA_-_February_2009.jpg)

Cemetery Chapel in 2009

The small budget dictated much of the production process.[\[46\]](#cite_note-Hardman/Eastmaninterview-48)[\[70\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewman200057-74) Scenes were filmed near [Evans City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evans_City,_Pennsylvania "Evans City, Pennsylvania"), Pennsylvania, 30 miles (48 km) north of Pittsburgh in rural [Butler County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butler_County,_Pennsylvania "Butler County, Pennsylvania");[\[71\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201046-75) the opening sequence was shot at the Evans City Cemetery on Franklin Road, south of the borough.[\[72\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201055–6-76)[\[e\]](#cite_note-79) Lacking the money to build or purchase a house for the main set, the filmmakers rented a nearby farmhouse scheduled for demolition. Though it lacked running water, some crew members slept there during the shooting, taking baths in a nearby creek.[\[75\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHervey200810–11-80) The building's neglected cellar was not a viable location for filming, so the few basement scenes were shot beneath The Latent Image offices.[\[76\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201028,_29,_59-81) The basement door shown in the film was cut into a wall by the production team and led nowhere.[\[77\]](#cite_note-82)

[Props](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatrical_property "Theatrical property") and [special effects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_effect "Special effect") were simple and limited by the budget. The blood, for example, was [Bosco Chocolate Syrup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosco_Chocolate_Syrup "Bosco Chocolate Syrup") drizzled over cast members' bodies.[\[78\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane2010n184-83) The human flesh consumed by ghouls consisted of meat and [offal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Offal "Offal") donated by an investor's butcher shop.[\[79\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHobermanRosenbaum1983121-84)[\[80\]](#cite_note-85) Zombie makeup varied during the film. Initially, makeup was limited to white skin with blackened eyes. As filming progressed, mortician's wax simulated wounds and decaying flesh.[\[81\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201047–49,_58-86) Filming took place between July 1967 and January 1968 under various titles. Work began under the generic working title *Monster Flick*, was changed to *Night of Anubis* after Romero's short story that provided the basis for the script, and was completed as *Night of the Flesh Eaters*, a title not used in the final release due to a potential conflict with a [similarly named film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Flesh_Eaters_\(film\) "The Flesh Eaters (film)").[\[82\]](#cite_note-Scrapbook,_Special_Features_2002-87)[\[83\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHeffernan2004219-88)[\[84\]](#cite_note-89) The small budget led Romero to shoot on [35 mm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/35mm_movie_film "35mm movie film") black-and-white film. The completed film ultimately benefited from the decision, as film historian [Joseph Maddrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Maddrey "Joseph Maddrey") describes the black-and-white filming as "[guerrilla-style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guerrilla_filmmaking "Guerrilla filmmaking")", resembling "the unflinching authority of a wartime newsreel". He found the [exploitation film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exploitation_film "Exploitation film") to resemble a documentary on social instability.[\[85\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMaddrey200451-90)

#### Directing

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Night_of_the_Living_Dead&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Directing")\]

[![Karen Cooper leans over her father's bloody corpse holding two handfuls of meat in a still from the film.](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/12/Living_dead_Karen_Cooper%2C_eating_her_father%27s_corpse_%28Night_of_the_Living_Dead%2C_1968%29.png/250px-Living_dead_Karen_Cooper%2C_eating_her_father%27s_corpse_%28Night_of_the_Living_Dead%2C_1968%29.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Living_dead_Karen_Cooper,_eating_her_father's_corpse_\(Night_of_the_Living_Dead,_1968\).png)

Living dead Karen Cooper, eating her father's corpse

*Night of the Living Dead* was the first feature-length film directed by George A. Romero. His initial work involved filming advertisements, industrial films, and [shorts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_film "Short film") for Pittsburgh public broadcaster [WQED](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WQED_\(TV\) "WQED (TV)")'s children's series *[Mister Rogers' Neighborhood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mister_Rogers'_Neighborhood "Mister Rogers' Neighborhood")*.[\[86\]](#cite_note-DOD-91)[\[87\]](#cite_note-92)[\[88\]](#cite_note-93) Romero's decision to direct *Night of the Living Dead* launched his career as a horror director. He took the helm of the sequels as well as *[Season of the Witch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Season_of_the_Witch_\(1972_film\) "Season of the Witch (1972 film)")* (1972), *[The Crazies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Crazies_\(1973_film\) "The Crazies (1973 film)")* (1973), *[Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_\(1978_film\) "Martin (1978 film)")* (1978), *[Creepshow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creepshow "Creepshow")* (1982) and *[The Dark Half](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dark_Half_\(film\) "The Dark Half (film)")* (1993).[\[89\]](#cite_note-94)[\[90\]](#cite_note-95) Critics saw the influence of the horror and science-fiction films of the 1950s in Romero's directorial style. Stephen Paul Miller, for instance, witnessed "a revival of fifties schlock shock ... and the army general's television discussion of military operations in the film echoes the often inevitable calling-in of the army in fifties horror films". Miller admits that "*Night of the Living Dead* takes greater relish in mocking these military operations through the general's pompous demeanor" and the government's inability to source the zombie epidemic or protect the citizenry.[\[91\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller199981-96) Romero described the film's intended mood as a downward arc from near hopelessness to complete tragedy. Film historian Carl Royer praised the film's sophistication—especially considering Romero's limited experience—and noted the use of [chiaroscuro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiaroscuro "Chiaroscuro") ([film noir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_noir "Film noir") style) lighting to create a mood of increasing alienation.[\[92\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyer200515-97)

*Night* was visually influenced by [Golden Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Age_of_Comic_Books "Golden Age of Comic Books") [horror comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horror_comics "Horror comics").[\[93\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChute198215-98) The [EC Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EC_Comics "EC Comics") books that Romero read as a child were graphic stories set in modern America. They often featured brutal deaths and reanimated corpses seeking revenge on the living.[\[94\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHervey200836-99) Romero said that he tried to bring into the film the "real hard shadows and weird angles and beautiful lighting that a comic book artist can create."[\[95\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESelby200443:40-100) He later collaborated with horror writer [Stephen King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_King "Stephen King") and former EC Comics artists on the homage *[Creepshow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creepshow "Creepshow")*.[\[96\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESelby200444:25-101)

***Night of the Living Dead*** is a 1968 American [zombie horror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zombie_horror "Zombie horror") film directed, photographed, and edited by [George A. Romero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_A._Romero "George A. Romero"), written by Romero and [John Russo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_A._Russo "John A. Russo"), and produced by [Russell W. Streiner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Streiner "Russell Streiner") and Karl Hardman. The [independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_film "Independent film") film's [ensemble cast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ensemble_cast "Ensemble cast")—which includes [Duane Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duane_Jones "Duane Jones"), [Judith O'Dea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_O'Dea "Judith O'Dea"), [Marilyn Eastman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marilyn_Eastman "Marilyn Eastman"), Karl Hardman, Judith Ridley, and Keith Wayne—star as a group of people trapped in a farmhouse in rural [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania"), under assault by flesh-eating [reanimated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undead "Undead") corpses. Although the monsters that appear in the film are referred to as "[ghouls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghoul "Ghoul")", they are credited with popularizing the modern portrayal of [zombies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zombie "Zombie") in popular culture.

Having gained experience creating television commercials, [industrial films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_film "Industrial film"), and *[Mister Rogers' Neighborhood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mister_Rogers'_Neighborhood "Mister Rogers' Neighborhood")* segments through their production company The Latent Image, Romero, Russo, and Streiner decided to make a horror film to capitalize on interest in the genre. Their script primarily drew inspiration from [Richard Matheson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Matheson "Richard Matheson")'s 1954 novel *[I Am Legend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Am_Legend_\(novel\) "I Am Legend (novel)")*. [Principal photography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_photography "Principal photography") took place between July 1967 and January 1968, mainly on location in [Evans City, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evans_City,_Pennsylvania "Evans City, Pennsylvania"), with Romero using [guerrilla filmmaking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guerrilla_filmmaking "Guerrilla filmmaking") techniques he had honed in his commercial and industrial work to complete the film on a [budget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_budgeting "Film budgeting") of approximately US$100,000. Unable to procure a proper set, the crew rented a condemned farmhouse to destroy during the course of filming.

*Night of the Living Dead* premiered in Pittsburgh on October 1, 1968\. It grossed US$12 million [domestically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_of_the_United_States "Cinema of the United States") and US$18 million internationally, earning more than 250 times its budget and making it one of the most profitable film productions of all time. Released shortly before the adoption of the [Motion Picture Association of America rating system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_Picture_Association_film_rating_system "Motion Picture Association film rating system"), the film's explicit violence and gore were considered groundbreaking, leading to controversy and negative reviews. It eventually garnered a [cult following](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult_film "Cult film") and critical acclaim, and has appeared on lists of [the greatest and most influential films ever made](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_films_considered_the_best "List of films considered the best") by such outlets as *[Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_\(magazine\) "Empire (magazine)")*, *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")* and *[Total Film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_Film "Total Film")*. Frequently identified as a touchstone in the development of the horror genre, retrospective scholarly analysis has focused on its reflection of the social and cultural changes in the United States during the 1960s, with particular attention towards the casting of Jones, an African-American, in the leading role.[\[6\]](#cite_note-Anarchy-8) In 1999, the film was deemed "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant" by the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") and selected for preservation in the [National Film Registry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Film_Registry "National Film Registry").[\[7\]](#cite_note-CNN-9)[\[8\]](#cite_note-PM-10)[\[9\]](#cite_note-11)

*Night of the Living Dead* created a successful [franchise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night_of_the_Living_Dead_\(film_series\) "Night of the Living Dead (film series)") that includes five following films released between 1978 and 2009, all directed by Romero. Since the film was mistakenly created without a [copyright notice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright_notice "Copyright notice"), it entered the [public domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_domain "Public domain") upon release,[\[10\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBolukLenz20115-12) resulting in numerous adaptations, [remakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remake "Remake"), and a lasting legacy in the horror genre. An [official remake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night_of_the_Living_Dead_\(1990_film\) "Night of the Living Dead (1990 film)"), written by Romero and directed by [Tom Savini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Savini "Tom Savini"), was released in 1990\.

## Plot

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Night_of_the_Living_Dead&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")\]

*Night of the Living Dead* (1968)

Siblings Barbra and Johnny Blair drive to a cemetery in rural [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania") to visit their father's grave, where a pale man in a tattered suit kills Johnny and attacks Barbra. Fleeing to a nearby farmhouse, she finds the resident's corpse lying half-eaten on the stairs. A growing horde of ghouls surrounds the house as a stranger, Ben, arrives and initially mistakes Barbra for the homeowner. After driving back several ghouls, he boards the windows and doors. A traumatized Barbra falls into a near catatonic state, forcing Ben to look after her. While searching the home for supplies, he locates a [lever-action rifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winchester_Model_1894 "Winchester Model 1894") upstairs.

Barbra is surprised to find people already taking shelter in the home's cellar. Harry Cooper, his wife Helen, and their young daughter Karen fled there after ghouls overturned their car and bit Karen on the arm, leaving her seriously ill. A teenage couple, Tom and Judy, took shelter after hearing an emergency broadcast while they were at a nearby lake. Tom and Ben secure the farmhouse while Harry protests that it is unsafe aboveground, before returning to the cellar. Tension rises in the group as more of the ghouls arrive to besiege the farmhouse.

Through radio and TV reports, the survivors learn that cannibalistic corpses, referred to as "ghouls", are reanimating and committing [mass murder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_murder "Mass murder") across the [East Coast of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Coast_of_the_United_States "East Coast of the United States") and that [posses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Posse_comitatus "Posse comitatus") of armed men are patrolling the countryside to exterminate the living dead. Reports confirm that the ghouls can die again from heavy blows to the head, bullets to the brain, or being burned. Various rescue centers offer refuge and safety, and scientists theorize that [radiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiation "Radiation") from an exploding [space probe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_probe "Space probe") returning from [Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus "Venus") caused the reanimations.

Ben devises a plan to obtain medical supplies for Karen and transport the group to a rescue center by refueling his truck at a pump on the farm. Ben, Tom, and Judy drive there together, holding the ghouls off with torches and [Molotov cocktails](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molotov_cocktail "Molotov cocktail"). However, spilled gasoline catches fire and causes the truck to explode, killing Tom and Judy. Ben makes it back, but when Harry refuses to unlock the door, Ben breaks it down.

The remaining survivors debate possible options, pausing when the 3 a.m. news broadcast airs. As they watch the update, the power fails, and the ghouls break through the doors and windows of the unlit home. In the chaos, Harry grabs Ben's gun to threaten him, but is disarmed and shot by Ben. Harry staggers down to the cellar and dies beside his daughter. Barbra awakens from her delirium and saves Helen from the ghouls, who then flees to the cellar.

Karen dies from her injuries, becomes a ghoul, feeds on her father's remains, and stabs her mother to death with a masonry [trowel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trowel "Trowel"). Barbra tries to help Ben keep the ghouls out, but freezes upon seeing the reanimated Johnny, who drags her into the horde. As the horde pours into the farmhouse, Ben retreats to the cellar, where he shoots the reanimated Harry and Helen.

In the morning, an armed posse arrives to dispatch the remaining ghouls. Awakened by their gunfire, Ben emerges from the cellar, but, mistaking him for a ghoul, the posse shoots him. His body is thrown onto a bonfire and burned with the other corpses.

The low-budget film featured no well-known actors,[\[11\]](#cite_note-Sandell2017-13) but it propelled several cast members' careers.[\[12\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane2010ch. 4-14) Two independent film companies from [Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh "Pittsburgh")—Hardman Associates and director [George A. Romero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_A._Romero "George A. Romero")'s The Latent Image—combined to form Image Ten, a production company chartered only to create *Night of the Living Dead*.[\[13\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201020–23-15) The cast consisted of members of Image Ten; actors previously cast in their commercials; clients who commissioned commercials; local TV, radio, and law enforcement; acquaintances of Romero, production crew and their relatives; and Pittsburgh stage actors.[\[14\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane2010ch. 4,_pp. 42–48-16)

- [Duane Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duane_Jones "Duane Jones") as Ben. The casting was potentially controversial in 1968 when it was rare for a black actor to be cast as the hero of an American film with a predominantly white cast, but Romero said Jones gave the best audition.[\[15\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones2005118-17) Jones later appeared in other films, including *[Ganja & Hess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganja_&_Hess "Ganja & Hess")* (1973) and *[Beat Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_Street "Beat Street")* (1984).[\[16\]](#cite_note-18)

- [Judith O'Dea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_O'Dea "Judith O'Dea") as Barbra Blair. A 23-year-old commercial and stage actress, O'Dea had previously worked for Hardman and Eastman in Pittsburgh. She was in Hollywood pursuing a film career when contacted about the role.[\[17\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECollum20043–9-19) O'Dea expressed surprise at the film's cultural impact and the recognition it brought her.[\[18\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECollum20044-20)

- [Russell Streiner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Streiner "Russell Streiner") as Johnny Blair, Barbra's brother. Streiner, Romero's business partner at The Latent Image, was one of the film's producers.[\[19\]](#cite_note-image-ten-streiner-21) In the film's credits, he is listed solely as a producer. Despite having no prior film acting experience,[\[20\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERusso198542-22) Streiner went on to act in and produce other films, notably the [1990 remake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night_of_the_Living_Dead_\(1990_film\) "Night of the Living Dead (1990 film)"), where he also had a cameo appearance as Sheriff McClelland.[\[19\]](#cite_note-image-ten-streiner-21)[\[21\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane2010-23)

- Karl Hardman as Harry Cooper. Hardman was president of Hardman Associates and one of the film's producers. Cooper's wife was played by Hardman's real-life business and romantic partner, Marilyn Eastman.[\[22\]](#cite_note-24)[\[23\]](#cite_note-Barnes2021-25) Hardman also remixed the film's sound track and created sound effects.[\[24\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201071–72-26)

- [Marilyn Eastman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marilyn_Eastman "Marilyn Eastman") as Helen Cooper.[\[25\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECollum20043-27) Vice president of Hardman Associates, Marilyn Eastman played Helen Cooper and the unnamed, bug-eating zombie. She later appeared in *[Santa Claws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Claws_\(1996_film\) "Santa Claws (1996 film)")* (1996), directed by [John Russo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_A._Russo "John A. Russo").[\[23\]](#cite_note-Barnes2021-25)[\[26\]](#cite_note-28)

- Kyra Schon as Karen Cooper. Hardman's daughter in real life,[\[27\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201042-29) nine-year-old Schon also portrayed the mangled corpse on the house's upper floor that Ben drags away.[\[28\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201043-30)

- Keith Wayne as Tom. "Keith Wayne" was Ronald Keith Hartman's stage name.[\[28\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201043-30) After this lone acting role, Wayne went on to work as a singer, dancer, musician, and night-club owner,[\[29\]](#cite_note-news.google.com-31)[\[28\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201043-30) before becoming a [chiropractor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiropractor "Chiropractor") in North Carolina.[\[29\]](#cite_note-news.google.com-31) Wayne explained the change in careers during a 1992 interview, "I am not that person anymore. \[...\] I got to a point in my life where I wanted to have some control. I didn't want to wake up at 40 or 50 and not be in control."[\[30\]](#cite_note-32) In 1995, he took his own life at age 50\.[\[31\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane2010204-33)[\[32\]](#cite_note-34)

- Judith Ridley as Judy. A 19-year-old receptionist from Hardman Associates, Ridley auditioned for Barbra without any acting experience and was given the less-demanding role of Judy.[\[33\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201042–43-35) Ridley starred in Romero's second feature *[There's Always Vanilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/There's_Always_Vanilla "There's Always Vanilla")* (1971).[\[34\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201090–92-36)

- [Bill Hinzman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Hinzman "Bill Hinzman") as the cemetery ghoul. Hinzman played the first ghoul encountered by Barbra and Johnny in the cemetery and later worked on several horror films including *[The Majorettes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Majorettes "The Majorettes")* (1986) and *[Flesheater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flesheater "Flesheater")* (1988).[\[35\]](#cite_note-37)[\[36\]](#cite_note-38)

- [George Kosana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Kosana "George Kosana") as Sheriff McClelland. Kosana also served as the film's [production manager](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_production_manager "Unit production manager").[\[37\]](#cite_note-:0-39)

- [Bill "Chilly Billy" Cardille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Cardille "Bill Cardille") as himself.[\[38\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201045-40) Cardille was well known in Pittsburgh as the [horror host](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horror_host "Horror host") of the anthology series *[Chiller Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiller_Theatre_\(Pittsburgh\) "Chiller Theatre (Pittsburgh)")*.[\[39\]](#cite_note-41) His daughter [Lori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lori_Cardille "Lori Cardille") later starred in Romero's *[Day of the Dead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day_of_the_Dead_\(1985_film\) "Day of the Dead (1985 film)")* (1985).[\[40\]](#cite_note-42)[\[41\]](#cite_note-43)

## Production

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Night_of_the_Living_Dead&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Production")\]

### Development and pre-production

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Night_of_the_Living_Dead&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Development and pre-production")\]

External videos

[![video icon](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/Nuvola_apps_kaboodle.svg/20px-Nuvola_apps_kaboodle.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nuvola_apps_kaboodle.svg) [The Calgon Story](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1oMQRrcLIaI) The creation of this high-budget [television commercial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_commercial "Television commercial") for [Calgon water softener](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calgon "Calgon") spurred the film's producers to create *Night of the Living Dead*.[\[42\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201028-44)

George Romero embarked upon his career in the [film industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_industry "Film industry") while attending [Carnegie Mellon University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Mellon_University "Carnegie Mellon University") in [Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh "Pittsburgh").[\[43\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201025-45) He directed and produced television commercials and [industrial films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sponsored_film "Sponsored film") for The Latent Image, a company he co-founded with his friend [Russell Streiner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Streiner "Russell Streiner").[\[44\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201026–27-46) The Latent Image started small, but after producing a high-budget [Calgon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calgon "Calgon") commercial spoofing *[Fantastic Voyage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fantastic_Voyage "Fantastic Voyage")* (1966), Romero felt that the company had the experience and equipment to produce a feature film.[\[42\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201028-44) They wanted to capitalize on the film industry's "thirst for the bizarre", according to Romero.[\[45\]](#cite_note-47) He, Streiner, and [John A. Russo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_A._Russo "John A. Russo") contacted Karl Hardman and Marilyn Eastman, president, and vice president respectively, of a Pittsburgh-based industrial film firm called Hardman Associates, Inc. The Latent Image pitched their idea for a then-untitled horror film.[\[46\]](#cite_note-Hardman/Eastmaninterview-48)

These discussions led to the creation of Image Ten, a production company chartered to produce a single feature film. The initial budget was $6,000;[\[13\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201020–23-15) each member of the production company invested $600 for a share of the profits.[\[47\]](#cite_note-49)[\[c\]](#cite_note-50) Ten more investors contributed another $6,000, but this was still insufficient.[\[48\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERusso19856–7-51) Production stopped multiple times during filming while Romero used early footage to persuade additional investors.[\[49\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPeary1981227-52) Image Ten eventually raised approximately $114,000 for the budget ($1,055,000 today).[\[50\]](#cite_note-inflation-US-53)[\[48\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERusso19856–7-51)

### Writing

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Night_of_the_Living_Dead&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Writing")\]

[![A group of actors in zombie makeup shamble across the unlit lawn of the farmhouse.](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/Zombies_NightoftheLivingDead.jpg/250px-Zombies_NightoftheLivingDead.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Zombies_NightoftheLivingDead.jpg)

Ghouls swarm around the house, searching for living [human flesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_cannibalism "Human cannibalism").

The script was co-written by Russo and Romero. They abandoned an early [horror comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horror_comedy_\(genre\) "Horror comedy (genre)") concept about adolescent aliens,[\[51\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201023-54) after realizing they would not have the budget to create a convincing spaceship.[\[52\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201021-55) Russo proposed a more constrained narrative where a young man runs away from home and discovers aliens harvesting human corpses for food in a cemetery.[\[53\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERusso198531,_61-56)[\[54\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201020–24-57) Romero combined this idea with an unpublished short story about flesh-eating ghouls,[\[55\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBishop2006199-58) and they began filming with an incomplete script.[\[49\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPeary1981227-52)[\[51\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201023-54) According to Russo, the screenplay written prior to filming only covered events up to the emergence of the Cooper family.[\[56\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESurmacz197516-59) Russo completed the script while filming and Romero later expanded the final pages of his short story into the sequels *[Dawn of the Dead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawn_of_the_Dead_\(1978_film\) "Dawn of the Dead (1978 film)")* (1978) and *[Day of the Dead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day_of_the_Dead_\(1985_film\) "Day of the Dead (1985 film)")* (1985).[\[57\]](#cite_note-60)

Romero drew inspiration from [Richard Matheson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Matheson "Richard Matheson")'s *[I Am Legend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Am_Legend_\(novel\) "I Am Legend (novel)")* (1954),[\[58\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDinello2006257-61)[\[d\]](#cite_note-62) a [horror novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horror_fiction "Horror fiction") about a [plague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epidemic "Epidemic") that ravages a futuristic Los Angeles. The infected in *I Am Legend* become [vampire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vampire "Vampire")\-like creatures and prey on the uninfected.[\[59\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPaffenroth2006138–143-63)[\[48\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERusso19856–7-51)[\[60\]](#cite_note-64) Matheson described Romero's interpretation as "kind of cornball",[\[61\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeaver1999307-65) and more theft than homage.[\[62\]](#cite_note-66) In an interview, Romero contrasted *Night of the Living Dead* with *I Am Legend*. He explained that Matheson wrote about the aftermath of a complete global upheaval; Romero wanted to explore how people would respond to that kind of disaster as it developed.[\[63\]](#cite_note-67)

Much of the dialogue was altered, rewritten, or improvised by the cast.[\[64\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201033–34,_40,_45-68) Lead actress Judith O'Dea told an interviewer, "I don't know if there was an actual working script! We would go over what basically had to be done, then just did it the way we each felt it *should* be done".[\[18\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECollum20044-20) One example offered by O'Dea concerns a scene where Barbra tells Ben about Johnny's death. O'Dea said that the script vaguely had Barbra talk about riding in the car with Johnny before they were attacked. She described Barbra's dialogue for the scene as entirely [improv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Improv_theater "Improv theater").[\[65\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECollum20043–4-69) Eastman modified the scenes written for Helen and Harry Cooper in the cellar.[\[46\]](#cite_note-Hardman/Eastmaninterview-48) Karl Hardman attributed Ben's lines to lead actor Duane Jones. Ben was an uneducated truck driver in the script until Jones began to rewrite his character.[\[66\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201032–35-70)[\[46\]](#cite_note-Hardman/Eastmaninterview-48)

The lead role was initially written for a [white](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_American "White American") actor, but upon casting black actor Duane Jones, Romero intentionally did not alter the script to reflect this.[\[67\]](#cite_note-Walkdead-71) The film appeared in theaters at a time when very few black actors played leading roles. The rare exceptions, like the consciously black heroes played by [Sidney Poitier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidney_Poitier "Sidney Poitier"), were written as subservient to make those characters palatable to white audiences.[\[68\]](#cite_note-72)[\[69\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarper2005-73) Asked in 2013 if he took inspiration from the [assassination of Martin Luther King Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Martin_Luther_King_Jr. "Assassination of Martin Luther King Jr.") in the same year that the movie was made, Romero responded in the negative, noting that he only heard about the shooting when he was on his way to find distribution for the finished film.[\[67\]](#cite_note-Walkdead-71)

### Filming

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Night_of_the_Living_Dead&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Filming")\]

#### Principal photography

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Night_of_the_Living_Dead&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Principal photography")\]

[![Color photograph of tombstones from the film.](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/EvansCityCemetery_PA.jpg/250px-EvansCityCemetery_PA.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:EvansCityCemetery_PA.jpg)

[Evans City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evans_City,_Pennsylvania "Evans City, Pennsylvania") Cemetery in 2007

[![Color photograph of the cemetery chapel seen in the film, now with all windows boarded over.](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f6/Evans_City_Cemetery_Chapel%2C_Evans_City%2C_PA_-_February_2009.jpg/250px-Evans_City_Cemetery_Chapel%2C_Evans_City%2C_PA_-_February_2009.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Evans_City_Cemetery_Chapel,_Evans_City,_PA_-_February_2009.jpg)

Cemetery Chapel in 2009

The small budget dictated much of the production process.[\[46\]](#cite_note-Hardman/Eastmaninterview-48)[\[70\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewman200057-74) Scenes were filmed near [Evans City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evans_City,_Pennsylvania "Evans City, Pennsylvania"), Pennsylvania, 30 miles (48 km) north of Pittsburgh in rural [Butler County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butler_County,_Pennsylvania "Butler County, Pennsylvania");[\[71\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201046-75) the opening sequence was shot at the Evans City Cemetery on Franklin Road, south of the borough.[\[72\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201055–6-76)[\[e\]](#cite_note-79) Lacking the money to build or purchase a house for the main set, the filmmakers rented a nearby farmhouse scheduled for demolition. Though it lacked running water, some crew members slept there during the shooting, taking baths in a nearby creek.[\[75\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHervey200810–11-80) The building's neglected cellar was not a viable location for filming, so the few basement scenes were shot beneath The Latent Image offices.[\[76\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201028,_29,_59-81) The basement door shown in the film was cut into a wall by the production team and led nowhere.[\[77\]](#cite_note-82)

[Props](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatrical_property "Theatrical property") and [special effects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_effect "Special effect") were simple and limited by the budget. The blood, for example, was [Bosco Chocolate Syrup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosco_Chocolate_Syrup "Bosco Chocolate Syrup") drizzled over cast members' bodies.[\[78\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane2010n184-83) The human flesh consumed by ghouls consisted of meat and [offal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Offal "Offal") donated by an investor's butcher shop.[\[79\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHobermanRosenbaum1983121-84)[\[80\]](#cite_note-85) Zombie makeup varied during the film. Initially, makeup was limited to white skin with blackened eyes. As filming progressed, mortician's wax simulated wounds and decaying flesh.[\[81\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKane201047–49,_58-86) Filming took place between July 1967 and January 1968 under various titles. Work began under the generic working title *Monster Flick*, was changed to *Night of Anubis* after Romero's short story that provided the basis for the script, and was completed as *Night of the Flesh Eaters*, a title not used in the final release due to a potential conflict with a [similarly named film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Flesh_Eaters_\(film\) "The Flesh Eaters (film)").[\[82\]](#cite_note-Scrapbook,_Special_Features_2002-87)[\[83\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHeffernan2004219-88)[\[84\]](#cite_note-89) The small budget led Romero to shoot on [35 mm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/35mm_movie_film "35mm movie film") black-and-white film. The completed film ultimately benefited from the decision, as film historian [Joseph Maddrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Maddrey "Joseph Maddrey") describes the black-and-white filming as "[guerrilla-style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guerrilla_filmmaking "Guerrilla filmmaking")", resembling "the unflinching authority of a wartime newsreel". He found the [exploitation film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exploitation_film "Exploitation film") to resemble a documentary on social instability.[\[85\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMaddrey200451-90)

#### Directing

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Night_of_the_Living_Dead&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Directing")\]

[![Karen Cooper leans over her father's bloody corpse holding two handfuls of meat in a still from the film.](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/12/Living_dead_Karen_Cooper%2C_eating_her_father%27s_corpse_%28Night_of_the_Living_Dead%2C_1968%29.png/250px-Living_dead_Karen_Cooper%2C_eating_her_father%27s_corpse_%28Night_of_the_Living_Dead%2C_1968%29.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Living_dead_Karen_Cooper,_eating_her_father's_corpse_\(Night_of_the_Living_Dead,_1968\).png)

Living dead Karen Cooper, eating her father's corpse

*Night of the Living Dead* was the first feature-length film directed by George A. Romero. His initial work involved filming advertisements, industrial films, and [shorts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_film "Short film") for Pittsburgh public broadcaster [WQED](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WQED_\(TV\) "WQED (TV)")'s children's series *[Mister Rogers' Neighborhood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mister_Rogers'_Neighborhood "Mister Rogers' Neighborhood")*.[\[86\]](#cite_note-DOD-91)[\[87\]](#cite_note-92)[\[88\]](#cite_note-93) Romero's decision to direct *Night of the Living Dead* launched his career as a horror director. He took the helm of the sequels as well as *[Season of the Witch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Season_of_the_Witch_\(1972_film\) "Season of the Witch (1972 film)")* (1972), *[The Crazies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Crazies_\(1973_film\) "The Crazies (1973 film)")* (1973), *[Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_\(1978_film\) "Martin (1978 film)")* (1978), *[Creepshow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creepshow "Creepshow")* (1982) and *[The Dark Half](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dark_Half_\(film\) "The Dark Half (film)")* (1993).[\[89\]](#cite_note-94)[\[90\]](#cite_note-95) Critics saw the influence of the horror and science-fiction films of the 1950s in Romero's directorial style. Stephen Paul Miller, for instance, witnessed "a revival of fifties schlock shock ... and the army general's television discussion of military operations in the film echoes the often inevitable calling-in of the army in fifties horror films". Miller admits that "*Night of the Living Dead* takes greater relish in mocking these military operations through the general's pompous demeanor" and the government's inability to source the zombie epidemic or protect the citizenry.[\[91\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller199981-96) Romero described the film's intended mood as a downward arc from near hopelessness to complete tragedy. Film historian Carl Royer praised the film's sophistication—especially considering Romero's limited experience—and noted the use of [chiaroscuro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiaroscuro "Chiaroscuro") ([film noir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_noir "Film noir") style) lighting to create a mood of increasing alienation.[\[92\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyer200515-97)

*Night* was visually influenced by [Golden Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Age_of_Comic_Books "Golden Age of Comic Books") [horror comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horror_comics "Horror comics").[\[93\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChute198215-98) The [EC Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EC_Comics "EC Comics") books that Romero read as a child were graphic stories set in modern America. They often featured brutal deaths and reanimated corpses seeking revenge on the living.[\[94\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHervey200836-99) Romero said that he tried to bring into the film the "real hard shadows and weird angles and beautiful lighting that a comic book artist can create."[\[95\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESelby200443:40-100) He later collaborated with horror writer [Stephen King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_King "Stephen King") and former EC Comics artists on the homage *[Creepshow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creepshow "Creepshow")*.[\[96\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESelby200444:25-101)

***The Exorcist III*** is a 1990 American [supernatural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supernatural_film "Supernatural film") [psychological horror film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychological_horror_\(film_and_television\) "Psychological horror (film and television)") written for the screen and directed by [William Peter Blatty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Peter_Blatty "William Peter Blatty"), based on his 1983 novel *[Legion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legion_\(Blatty_novel\) "Legion (Blatty novel)")*. It is the third installment in [*The Exorcist* film series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Exorcist_\(franchise\) "The Exorcist (franchise)") and the final installment in Blatty's "Trilogy of Faith" after *[The Ninth Configuration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ninth_Configuration "The Ninth Configuration")* (1980), serving as a follow-up and direct sequel of *[The Exorcist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Exorcist "The Exorcist")* (1973). The film stars [George C. Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_C._Scott "George C. Scott"), [Ed Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Flanders "Ed Flanders"), [Jason Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Miller_\(playwright\) "Jason Miller (playwright)"), [Scott Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Wilson_\(actor\) "Scott Wilson (actor)"), [Nicol Williamson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicol_Williamson "Nicol Williamson"), and [Brad Dourif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brad_Dourif "Brad Dourif").

The film follows a character from the original film, Lieutenant William F. Kinderman, who investigates a series of demonic murders in [Georgetown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgetown,_Washington,_D.C. "Georgetown, Washington, D.C.") that have the hallmarks of the Gemini, a deceased serial killer. Blatty based aspects of the Gemini Killer on the real-life [Zodiac Killer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zodiac_Killer "Zodiac Killer"),[\[4\]](#cite_note-4) although there is no evidence of interest in this film by The Zodiac Killer*.*[\[5\]](#cite_note-SFGateZL2-5)[\[6\]](#cite_note-6)[\[7\]](#cite_note-7)

Blatty, who wrote [*The Exorcist* novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Exorcist_\(novel\) "The Exorcist (novel)") and the screenplay for its 1973 film adaptation, conceived *The Exorcist III* with *The Exorcist* director [William Friedkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Friedkin "William Friedkin") attached to direct. When Friedkin left the project, Blatty adapted the script into the 1983 novel *Legion*. [Morgan Creek Productions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgan_Creek_Productions "Morgan Creek Productions") bought the [film rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_rights "Film rights"), with Blatty as director. Initially designed to be a standalone adaptation of that novel (hence the anachronistic elements which contradict Friedkin's adaptation of *The Exorcist*), the final cut wound up being an official entry in the filmed series due to Morgan Creek demanding extensive last-minute changes — including the insistence of bringing back a key cast member from the 1973 film, as well as an exorcism sequence for the climax — much to Blatty's frustration.[\[8\]](#cite_note-A_Legion_of_Interference-8) Though some of the original footage appears [permanently lost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lost_film "Lost film"), [Scream Factory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scream_Factory "Scream Factory") released a [director's cut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director's_cut "Director's cut") closer to Blatty's vision in 2016, with footage assembled from various sources.[\[9\]](#cite_note-NinthConf-9)[\[10\]](#cite_note-10)

*The Exorcist III* was released in the United States on August 17, 1990, by [20th Century Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th_Century_Fox "20th Century Fox"). The film grossed $44 million domestically against a production budget of $11 million and received mixed reviews from critics.[\[11\]](#cite_note-:0-11) However, the film gained a cult following over time and is now largely considered the best sequel of the franchise.[\[12\]](#cite_note-12)

## Plot

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Exorcist_III&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")\]

In [Georgetown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgetown_\(Washington,_D.C.\) "Georgetown (Washington, D.C.)"), fifteen years after [Regan MacNeil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regan_MacNeil "Regan MacNeil")'s exorcism in 1973,[\[a\]](#cite_note-Year-13) Father Joseph Dyer and Lieutenant William F. Kinderman reminisce about Father [Damien Karras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damien_Karras "Damien Karras"). The following night, an incident at a church occurs indicating the presence of something supernatural, which causes the [Christ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus "Jesus") figure on a crucifix to open its eyes. A man walking on the street speaks about a dream of "falling down a long flight of steps", suggesting that someone is committing murders linked to Karras' death.

The next morning, Kinderman is called to the scene of a murder. Thomas Kintry, a black youth, has had his head replaced with the head from a statue of Jesus. Afterwards, a priest, Father Kanavan, is murdered in the confessional one night, and is also decapitated. The fingerprints at the crime scenes do not match, indicating different people committed each murder. Dyer falls ill and ends up in hospital which houses a psychiatric ward for the elderly. He is also murdered and decapitated with all of his blood neatly placed in small bottles. After questioning patients in the mental ward, assisted by Sergeant Mel Atkins, Kinderman notices that the murders fit the [modus operandi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modus_operandi "Modus operandi") of James Venamun, "The Gemini Killer", a serial killer who was executed fifteen years earlier.

Kinderman questions another patient at the hospital, elderly Mrs. Clelia, who knows nothing of Dyer's murder. He then visits the head of a psychiatric ward, Dr. Temple, who relates the history of one of his patients. The patient was found wandering aimlessly fifteen years previously with [amnesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amnesia "Amnesia"). He was locked up, [catatonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catatonia "Catatonia") until six weeks ago when he became lucid and violent, claiming to be the Gemini Killer. The patient is Kinderman's old friend Damien Karras, who is in fact possessed by Venamun. The Gemini Killer expresses ignorance of Karras, but boasts of murdering Father Dyer and the other victims years ago. After his appearance changes to that of the Gemini Killer, he threatens to punish Kinderman if the paper doesn't report the Gemini Killer is still killing.

Kinderman visits Father Riley, the head of the church council that Kanavan and Dyer worked for and that Kanavan himself ran fifteen years earlier. When discussing a connection between the murders, Kinderman believes the suspect to be possessed by the Gemini Killer and questions Riley on his belief in possessions. Riley suggests he talk to Father Paul Morning, who handled an exorcism in the Philippines and that "his hair turned white overnight" as a result. Riley reveals a connection between the victims regarding the Regan MacNeil case: Kanavan allowing that exorcism to take place, Dyer being friends with the MacNeil family, and Kintry's mother being the one who decoded a backwards message on a tape recording of [Pazuzu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pazuzu_\(The_Exorcist\) "Pazuzu (The Exorcist)") – the entity who possessed Regan.

That night, Nurse Amy Keating is murdered, and Dr. Temple dies by suicide. Kinderman returns to see Karras who is still possessed by the Gemini Killer. The killer explains that he is being aided by "The Master", presumably Pazuzu, who was vengeful for Karras expelling him from Regan's body. "The Master" took the spirit of Venamun (who was executed the same night), and placed it in Karras's body with Karras' spirit locked inside to witness the horrific acts as punishment. The Gemini Killer has possessed other people in the institution to carry out his murders and forced Dr. Temple to help him.

The Gemini Killer possesses another elderly patient, who leaves the hospital disguised as a nurse and attempts to murder Kinderman and his family at their home. The attack abruptly ends when Father Morning arrives at the hospital to confront Karras, having sensed a calling to perform another exorcism. As he attempts to cleanse Karras, "The Master" intervenes, taking over Karras' body, and Morning is severely mutilated. Kinderman rushes back to the hospital with the now unconscious patient and attempts to euthanize Karras. The possessed Karras then torments and attempts to kill Kinderman.

As "The Master" chants how victory is on his side, Father Morning regains consciousness and tells Karras to fight. The real Karras briefly regains his free will and cries out to Kinderman to shoot and kill him. Kinderman does this, freeing Karras from both the Gemini Killer and his "Master". Later, Kinderman and Sergeant Atkins watch Karras' funeral, his tombstone listing his death at the age of 40 on October 9, 1975\.
